extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, students, and general readers interested in regulation and public policy
extracted.subtask_description: A conceptual framework for assessing whether a proposed regulation actually serves the general public or instead advances special interests; emphasizes empirical comparison of benefits and costs and attention to political incentives. Useful for analysts, commentators, and citizens judging regulatory proposals (example: Uber/TfL proposals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest standard: regulations should improve consumer welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulators will implement rules which improve the welfare of consumers; regulations are meant to protect consumers from harm resulting from irresponsible, greedy, or fraudulent producers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the stated purpose of the regulation is to maximise private citizens' benefits (e.g., TfL's framing that new rules could 'raise standards' and 'ensure Londoners can continue to benefit'). Check whether the regulation explicitly aims at consumer protection and whether that aim is plausible given available evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory benefits must be demonstrable and justify costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed regulations should offer clear benefits to citizens; if a rule does not offer clear benefits, the public-interest justification is weak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the claimed benefits to observable measures (e.g., current average wait times, price, or service availability). Question rules that reduce services or convenience (example: a mandatory five-minute wait when current average is three minutes). Treat lack of clear consumer benefit as a red flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political-economy test: consider incentives and influence of self-interested actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations emerge in a political environment populated by self-interested actors (public and private); actors with the ability to influence regulators will attempt to shape rules for their own benefit (Stigler's framework).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess who has the motive and capacity to influence rulemaking. Ask whether the regulation aligns with the interests of politically connected or organized groups rather than the diffuse public. Look for indirect signs of capture (lobbying, industry involvement in consultations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Who benefits? Distinguish special-interest protections from general-interest gains
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether a regulation primarily benefits a narrow, concentrated group (special interests) rather than the general public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the likely beneficiaries (e.g., taxi drivers) and weigh their concentrated gains against the losses borne by many consumers. Use concrete examples: rules that protect incumbent providers from competition (e.g., banning app features) likely benefit incumbents at public expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on consumer information and choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the regulation increases or decreases the information available to consumers and whether it restricts consumer choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess provisions that limit transparency (e.g., preventing apps from showing available cars) or restrict new service models (e.g., banning ridesharing). Reduced information/options are harms to consumers and should count against the regulation unless offset by safety or other demonstrable gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on competition and prices
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the regulation reduces competition and thereby raises monetary and non-monetary costs to consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare prices and service options pre- and post-regulation where data exist (example table comparing black cab vs Uber fares). Treat rules that shield incumbents from competitive pressures as likely to raise prices and worsen service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on innovation and entrepreneurial activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the regulation raises costs and risks for entrepreneurs, thereby reducing innovation and the development of better services for consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether compliance burdens, entry barriers, or restrictive rules deter new entrants or novel service models. Weigh these long-term dynamic costs when judging the regulation's net public benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributional pattern: concentrated benefits versus dispersed costs and mobilization likelihood
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine how costs and benefits are distributed; concentrated beneficiaries are more likely to organize and influence policy than widely dispersed small losers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the size and organization of beneficiary groups (e.g., 20,000 black cab drivers) versus the diffuse population of consumers. Consider recent mobilization evidence (e.g., petitions, protests) as part of the political calculus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider voter influence and political feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulators consider not only firms' influence but also voter sentiment; where voters strongly oppose a proposal it is less likely to pass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess public opinion and organized consumer responses (e.g., petitions, protests) as factors that can counterbalance special-interest influence. Use this as part of both explaining regulatory outcomes and predicting feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use empirical evidence and concrete examples when evaluating regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ground judgments about regulations in observable data (wait times, price comparisons, case examples) rather than solely in abstract claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and present empirical measures relevant to the regulation's stated goals (service quality, price, congestion effects). Use these data to test whether the regulation's benefits outweigh its costs and to reveal if stated consumer-protection rationales are plausible.
